title: Quantum sensors that compute: quantum computational magnetic-field sensing using a superconducting qubit
authors: Purnendu Sen, Mathieu Ouellet, Saeed A. Khan, Wayne Wang, Sridhar Prabhu, Alen Senanian, William P. Banner, William D. Oliver, Peter L. McMahon
abstract: A measurement of a single-qubit quantum sensor reveals at most 1 bit of information about the signal that was sensed. To perform a classification task on the signal, the conventional approach is to repeat a sensing protocol many times, averaging the measurement results to obtain a high-precision estimate of the sensed signal, and then to apply classical postprocessing. Quantum computational sensing (QCS) is an alternative approach that breaks with the paradigm of first obtaining a classical estimate of the signal and then computing a function of the estimated signal in postprocessing. QCS instead combines quantum sensing with quantum computing to concentrate information about the signal relevant to the task into the solitary bit revealed by each measurement. Here, we report on the experimental demonstration of QCS where sensing and computing were both performed by the same single superconducting transmon qubit. We consider various binary classification tasks based on static and oscillating magnetic fields induced by current through a flux line. The fields were sensed through a double-junction superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) loop that was part of the qubit. We used a protocol based on quantum signal processing to preprocess the sensed signals in the quantum domain prior to measurement. For tasks on static magnetic fields, our protocol outperformed the conventional baseline of Ramsey-based phase estimation by as much as 15 percentage points. For tasks on oscillating magnetic fields, we classified signal amplitude and frequency with up to 20 and 15 percentage points higher accuracy, respectively, compared to the conventional baseline of optimized dynamical-decoupling protocols. Our results illustrate how quantum computing can enhance quantum sensing even with a minimally sized quantum system subject to the practical limitations of decoherence and error-prone operations.
summary: This work demonstrates Quantum Computational Sensing (QCS) using a superconducting transmon qubit to enhance magnetic-field sensing. Instead of classically estimating the signal first, QCS embeds the required computation directly into the quantum measurement process. The results show that this approach significantly boosts classification accuracy compared to standard quantum sensing techniques, even when considering practical noise limitations.
main_problem: The paper addresses the limitation of conventional quantum sensing, which requires classical post-processing after estimating a signal, by proposing Quantum Computational Sensing (QCS). QCS aims to combine sensing and computation to directly extract task-specific information into the measurement outcome.
main_result: The experimental demonstration showed that QCS significantly outperforms conventional sensing baselines for binary classification tasks on both static and oscillating magnetic fields, achieving up to 20% higher accuracy in amplitude classification.
method: The authors utilize a protocol based on quantum signal processing (QSP) to preprocess sensed signals in the quantum domain, encoding task-relevant information into the measurement basis before measurement.
model_or_system: The physical platform is a superconducting transmon qubit, used to sense magnetic fields via an integrated double-junction superconducting quantum interference device (SQUID) loop. The protocols compare QCS against optimized Dynamical-Decoupling (DD) methods.
key_observables: Classification Accuracy (%), Cosine Similarity, Mutual Information, and the final $\langle z angle$ distribution.
important_parameters: Signal amplitude and frequency ranges, interrogation times ($T$), and readout fidelity.
main_assumptions: The QCS protocols are non-adaptive (control parameters fixed before data acquisition), and the comparison is made under practical limitations of decoherence and readout errors.
figures_summary: Figures compare QCS vs. conventional approaches for classification tasks (static/oscillating fields), show Pareto fronts illustrating resource trade-offs, and analyze the robustness of protocols against readout errors.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from introducing the QCS concept over classical estimation, demonstrating its application to static and oscillating field classification, and finally comparing QCS performance against optimized DD protocols using information-theoretic measures.
why_interesting: It provides a concrete, hardware-based demonstration of how quantum computation can be integrated into sensing protocols to achieve super-classical performance gains, which is highly relevant for quantum sensing applications in AMO physics.
